Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The R package lfda enables users to perform LFDA kernel N-dimensional reduction and obtain visualizations of the reduced data set using a 3D plotting function in R.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its ability to efficiently leverage vast amounts of demonstration data from unstructured observations. Unlike unconstrained learning tasks, robot movements are constrained by hardware limitations and the presence of hard boundaries that cannot be penetrated. These constraints pose significant challenges for imitation learning algorithms in adapting to new environments and ensuring the safety of the learned trajectory. Current methods lack the ability to account for nonlinear constraints and learn from demonstrations that include intentional avoidance actions. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel imitation learning framework called EKMP, capable of handling complex constraints, learning from demonstrations in new environments, and accounting for nonlinear safety constraints in its policy update. EKMP is evaluated through a series of experiments, including its application in learning to navigate a complex robotic arm within a constrained three-dimensional space, using only cross-sectional avoidance demonstrations, and in a two-robot coordination task, where the robots must avoid each other.

We have analytically confirmed the conformal bootstrap hypothesis for a specific part of the one-loop four-gluon amplitude in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, specifically the "central-emission vertex". This particular component of the amplitude is responsible for describing how gluons interact as they pass close to each other while traveling in opposite directions, after which they continue on their original paths. We took a novel approach to studying this vertex by transforming it into a function of several cross-ratios that arise from the removal of supersymmetric scales. In doing so, we found that this function, when mapped onto a specific region of the conformal space, is non-zero. We utilized the bootstrap approach to demonstrate that this function must be part of a larger function that, when subjected to certain constraints, satisfies specific requirements defined by the S-matrix conservation and the symmetry of the conformal group, particularly when studying a particular component of the super-amplitude. We were also able to derive this vertex from a set of helicity-amplitude components, after which we applied a particular transformation to obtain the one-loop amplitude itself.

To investigate topological superconductivity in one-dimensional systems with spin-orbit coupling, we developed a Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions. Using a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation hybrid method, we analyzed the model's phase diagram and found that spin-orbit coupling weakens the Mott-Hubbard instability, while strong coupling and certain electron hoppings induce highly stable one-dimensional topological phases through alloy disorder. These phases emerge when the chemical potential is positioned within the Mott-Hubbard gap and are characterized by one-dimensional topological singularities and Andreev points along the Fermi surface. Additionally, we found that the Rashba parameter has a minimal impact on the one-dimensional topological superconductivity and that the corresponding zero-energy bound states can be used as the basis for a one-dimensional version of the Majorana fuse box.

By using small-angle neutron scattering and magnetic torque magnetometry, we detected a previously unobserved transition in the Vortices Lattice of YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-x}$ at very low magnetic fields. The transition was found to occur at a specific temperature, $T^*$, which is close to one half of the VLT temperature $T_{\textrm{VLT}}$, and is characterized by a sudden rearrangement of the vortex lattice from a regular square pattern to a more randomly aligned state. The transition is more pronounced in higher quality samples and it is accompanied by a significant increase in the vortex elastic properties. The results suggest that the VLT and the square-square transition are both related to the decoupling of the Cu-O planes in the YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-x}$ material and that the latter could be a general feature of high-$T_c$ cuprates.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, such as nanoparticles, and fails to account for edge effects near the brush's termination. This paper proposes a new theory to address these limitations. It starts by assuming a highly stretched brush with a smoothly transitioning zone from the excluded region to the attached polymers. This transition is so slight that it can be represented by a linear approximation. Based on this assumption, the paper derives a new equation for estimating the inner excluded zone's size in curved, stretched brush configurations, including those with sharp edges. According to the proposed theory, edge effects can lead to surface tension variations, potentially causing the formation of molten brush patterns. This prediction is supported by simulation data and suggests that the theory can be applied across a broad range of brush curvatures.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers are using the Fermi Large Area Telescope (FAT) data to create all-sky maps of gamma-ray radiation, but these maps are currently limited by the long duration of Fermi's operations. With a satellite in orbit for over a decade, it's essential to update these maps frequently to avoid the influence of permanent sources. Machine learning algorithms can be trained on a vast dataset of gamma-ray observations to identify patterns and eliminate unwanted sources from the data, effectively creating more detailed all-sky maps. This approach can be particularly useful for analyzing time-variable sources, such as active galactic nuclei, which account for the majority of gamma-ray radiation in the sky. By updating the all-sky maps efficiently, scientists can efficiently update their understanding of the gamma-ray sky.

When making a series of independent decisions, a group of self-interested individuals can collaborate by taking a serial dictatorship approach, where each decision maker prioritizes the outcome that maximizes the next person's payoff. This study assesses the performance of this cooperative strategy in scenarios where decisions impact multiple independent payoffs. It establishes a general framework for analyzing the effectiveness of serial dictatorships in optimizing combined payoffs and applies this framework to examine cooperative equilibria in scenarios involving competition and auctions. It also explores the conditions under which a serially cooperative approach can lead to socially optimal outcomes and identifies specific scenarios in which it performs better than alternative cooperative solutions. Furthermore, it provides a solution for a particular class of combinatorial auctions and demonstrates the relevance of its findings to broader applications in combinatorial auctions and decision making under uncertainty.

We have conducted a comprehensive search for binary asteroids using Pan-STARRS1 archival images. Our findings include 22 confirmed binary asteroid systems along with 13 potential candidates. This total exceeds the number of binary asteroid discoveries made through adaptive optics by a significant margin. We calculated the orbital periods for 14 binary systems, including the known binary asteroid pairs 87 Sylvania and 3200 Phaethon. We used two independent methods to estimate the minimum possible separations for unsolved systems, and found that there are likely numerous binary asteroids with separations greater than 10 km. We also found that binary asteroid systems have a much higher fraction of low-eccentricity orbits than non-binary asteroids.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions of the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal detector and a suboptimal detector, and derive closed-form bounds on the distortion metric. A method for optimizing the transmission strategy is also presented, along with numerical examples and a real-world implementation using a pilot-assisted decoder.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Vue.js for the frontend and Flask for the backend, using
JavaScript and Python programming languages. Each tool is designed to visualize
galaxy SEDs, AGN SEDs, foregrounds, cosmological large-scale structures, and other
entities found in the RCSED2 catalog. We've made the tools publicly available to
facilitate easy access to the catalog's visualizations.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing publicly available gravity data and a 2.5D density model, researchers from the University of Alberta have identified the rift basin's boundary with the African continental margin.  They used this boundary to update the boundary with the South American continental margin based on gravity data and a 3D density model.  Their findings indicate the western boundary of the rift basin is a curved line influenced by the Roncador Fault and the Amazonas Basin.  It extends from 2 degrees South latitude to 32 degrees South latitude and 19 degrees West to 38 degrees West longitude.  Further, they found the rift basin's boundary with the African continental margin is more complex, characterized by several faults including the Roncador, Pelotas, and Rio Grande do Sul Faults.  They developed a 2D cross-sectional model of the rift basin along a profile from the continental slope to the equator.  It shows a 6 km thick sedimentary layer in the South Atlantic abyssal plain and 10 km in the Rio Grande Rise. A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
self-supervised learning, which involves simultaneously conducting both
unsupervised learning and supervised learning in an alternating manner.  The
process involves creating tasks that promote the extraction of meaningful
information from the data during the unsupervised training phase. Notably, a
common issue arises when the data is processed in an image-processing pipeline
due to the repeated transformation of image data, which hinders the effective
use of boundary information. This problem is particularly pronounced in
medical segmentation tasks.  To tackle this challenge, a novel unsupervised
learning approach called Boundary-aware Information Maximization (BIM) has
been developed to make the most of boundary information. The proposed BIM
framework leverages the information-maximization principle to push the model
to accurately extract meaningful information from the data during the unsupervised
training phase.  To make the most of the data during the unsupervised
training phase, the BIM framework utilizes two information-maximization
strategies, namely, information maximization and contrastive information

We introduce a groundbreaking approach to creating an on-line Dungeon Masters (DMs) using Artificial Intelligence (AI). We transform the popular Dungeons and Dragons role-playing game into a learning platform for multiple players, where the objective is for the players to achieve a common goal while the AI DM guides them through complex problem-solving tasks. To achieve this, we develop a novel method for training conversational AI to consider the perspectives of others, using a dataset of conversational D&D sessions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by showing that players can complete the adventure significantly faster when guided by our AI DM than by a human DM. We also highlight the significance of incorporating Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in the AI DM by highlighting the fact that players often fail to complete the adventure when guided by a human DM who lacks ToM. ToM enables the AI DM to anticipate the players' actions, present relevant information, and provide clear instructions, ultimately enabling the players to successfully complete the adventure.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to discovering rigid patterns of related words. In contrast, our proposed framework uses Machine Learning and Information Theory measures to identify clusters of words with dynamic relationships, enabling the discovery of flexible patterns of related words undergoing semantic change over time. In experiments using the LSCD2019 dataset, our method outperformed existing strategies and achieved superior results in evaluating semantic change patterns in multiple word clusters.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. In line with the Boer-Mulders function, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to the interaction between partons and the medium within a nucleon or nucleus.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the identification of distinct folding paths starting from the native states of knotted proteins. This method involves tracking the movement of specific protein segments through space and time, allowing researchers to pinpoint the formation of knots along the folding trajectory. By applying this approach to a set of knotted proteins in silico, as well as analyzing experimental data from biologists, the study reveals that the folding paths are unique to each knot type and suggest that the formation of knots occurs early in the folding process. Furthermore, the formation of knots appears to hinder the formation of protein folds in other arrangements, a finding that has implications for our understanding of the intricate relationship between protein knots, folds, and folding pathways.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence power spectrum measurements. Employing a profile likelihood method to eliminate bias, we found a narrow range for the EDE fraction $\Omega_{\rm EDE}/\Omega_{m} < 0.047$ at 68% confidence, which reduces the degeneracy associated with volume effects. This constraint significantly improves current limitations, providing a more precise understanding of EDE and its potential resolution to the Hubble tension.

Given that it fulfills the requirements for a high degree and a specific level of diffeomorphism invariance, we can determine a well-defined integer $m$ such that the symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $\big(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^3\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\

A detailed explanation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is provided, 
along with a clarification of commonly misunderstood concepts within the theorem's framework. A dichotomy exists, dividing the theorem's theory into two categories: those with symmetry fully preserved and those with symmetry fully broken. If the symmetry is fully preserved, there are no NG bosons present; in contrast, if the symmetry is fully broken, NG bosons do appear. However, in cases of partial symmetry breaking, characteristics of both categories emerge, resulting in the formation of massive vector bosons and the disappearance of NG bosons. A comparison with the Salam-Weinberg model serves as an example of this phenomenon.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the current methodological framework for generating counterfactual data is largely task-agnostic and relies on manual specification of variables, which severely limits scaling to complex tasks involving multiple variables. In our research, we introduce a novel, fully automated approach to generating counterfactual data for the test set in a single pass. This approach leverages a large language model to generate high-quality counterfactual contexts, which are distilled into labels by the model itself. We further develop an efficient framework to produce a robust counterfactual distribution, which can be achieved in a single pass without the need to store the entire distilled dataset. When evaluated on the NYU V2 dataset, our method yields a 6.5% improvement in accuracy over the baseline model and a 5% improvement in robust accuracy when subjected to perturbations. Moreover, our method exhibits a 10-fold reduction in costs when compared to traditional methods.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on graphene/sapphire substrates has yielded significant breakthroughs, however the underlying growth physics remains poorly understood. This study utilizes advanced analytical tools to reveal the intricate mechanisms behind remote epitaxy. By examining the anisotropic strain distribution in graphene, and the distribution of electrons within the Graphene/Heusler interface, our findings indicate that epitaxial relationships can be accurately predicted using two parameters: the lattice mismatch between Heusler films and the average graphene lattice, as well as the angle between Heusler films and the orientation of graphene. Through this understanding, researchers are now able to control the epitaxial balance between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy by adjusting the orientation of Heusler films in relation to graphene, effectively expanding the possibilities of remote epitaxy beyond existing limitations.

This paper introduces a novel code category, $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which can be seen as a variation of Hermitian codes over the residue class field $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}\cong \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$, resulting from combining two different $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear subspaces. We investigate the rank and kernel dimensions of these codes, establishing a link between the rank and kernel dimensions similar to that of classical linear codes. Furthermore, this paper presents a decomposition approach for $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes and provides an example illustrating this concept.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile to maximize oil recovery, compared to a static polymer flood model. Using the Koval model
as an example, they have calculated the benefits of using a graded viscosity bank over a static
polymer flood, finding that even a simple trapezoidal bank can increase oil recovery by 11% more
than not using polymers at all, and a more complex exponential bank can increase it by 13%.

When working with a large number of examples, each associated with one or more labels, 
the process of assigning all relevant labels to each example is referred to as a multi-label 
learning task. In contrast, the task addressed in this research involves working with a 
different kind of dataset, where each example is linked to only a single label. The term 
used to describe this kind of dataset is single positive (SP) datasets, characterized by 
the presence of a specific relevant label while excluding all other labels. Due to the 
absence of a key characteristic (multiple relevant labels), the traditional multi-label 
learning algorithms are ineffective in handling SP datasets effectively. To address this 
challenge, this research proposes an innovative method called the multi-label learner 
from single positive (MLSP) framework. The MLSP framework leverages a dataset that 
includes multiple positive labels, where all examples linked to a specific query label 
are selectively extracted and used as input. The framework's underlying assumption is 
that the relationships between the query label and all other relevant labels are similar 
in nature to the relationships between the query label and the remaining irrelevant 
labels. As a result, the framework is able to learn a multi-label classifier that can 
predict all other relevant labels with a high degree of accuracy and exclude the 
irrelevant labels. To evaluate the MLSP framework's performance, this research also 
introduces a new multi-label learning algorithm called the multi-label learner from SP
